James and William die during the defence and destruction of the city, buying time for Patrick's army and civilians to withdraw. Roo's fortune and trading network are consumed in the emergency he prepared for; Erik becomes one of the commanders holding the retreat together through Ravensburg and Darkmoor. Fadawah's advance is checked, not eliminated, and Duko remains with an occupying force in the west, so the human war continues beyond the book. The supernatural purpose of the invasion is exposed: the woman Jorna, Miranda's mother, has been presented as the Emerald Queen and used as a vessel in the Pantathians' attempt to restore Alma-Lodaka, while Jakan's traffic with the demon realm has opened a greater danger involving the demon king Maarg. Pug, Miranda, Nakor, Calis, and Tomas prevent that power from taking Midkemia and deny the Pantathians their intended triumph. Miranda is the daughter of Jorna and Macros the Black, and Macros returns in a renewed body, adding an old guardian to the damaged world's defenders. The invasion has been blunted, but the Western Realm remains occupied and must be reclaimed.
recaps.in_short: The Emerald Queen's fleet invades the Kingdom despite years of warning. Roo converts his merchant fortune into supplies and transport, Erik helps command the defence, and Duke James and William prepare Krondor for a battle they know may end in evacuation and destruction. Fadawah's disciplined armies force the Kingdom eastward; Krondor falls after James and William die buying time, while Erik helps preserve the retreat through Ravensburg and Darkmoor. Roo survives but much of the commercial world he built is consumed by war. Pug, Miranda, Nakor, Calis, and Tomas pursue the invasion's hidden purpose. The Emerald Queen is exposed as Jorna, Miranda's mother and a vessel in the Pantathians' plan to restore Alma-Lodaka, while Jakan's dealings reveal a still greater threat from the demon king Maarg. The crossing is stopped, and Miranda is revealed as the daughter of Jorna and Macros the Black as Macros returns in renewed form. Fadawah is checked but not destroyed, Duko still holds conquered territory, and the Kingdom faces the task of retaking the west.

recaps.text: Previously, in the Serpentwar Saga: Erik von Darkmoor and Rupert Avery were condemned for the death of Erik's abusive half-brother, secretly spared, and trained for Calis's reconnaissance company. In Novindus they found the Emerald Queen's forces conquering a continent to prepare an invasion of the Kingdom. Calis is the son of Tomas and the elven queen Aglaranna, joining human and elven blood to the Valheru inheritance Tomas carries from Ashen-Shugar. Pug and Tomas, once the young heroes of the Riftwar, are now elder guardians confronting dangers that cross worlds. Erik stayed in royal service after returning; Roo became a merchant prince in Krondor, using his foreknowledge of war to build both a fortune and a supply network. Roo's ambition damaged his marriage to Karli through his involvement with Sylvia Esterbrook. Fadawah has completed the enemy fleet. Pug's investigation, aided by the secretive magician Miranda and the Isalani wanderer Nakor, has confirmed that demonic power stands behind part of the campaign, though the Emerald Queen's true identity and the Pantathians' final purpose remain concealed.

Krondor prepares for an invasion many of its residents still experience mainly as rumours, shortages, and military demands. Duke James and Prince Patrick organise the Western Realm while William commands its soldiers. Erik helps turn Calis's intelligence into practical defence and Roo places warehouses, shipping contacts, and credit at the Kingdom's disposal. Queg and the sea routes matter because the approaching war will be decided as much by transport as by battle. At the same time Pug and Miranda compare what they know of demons and rifts. Their alliance is real but incomplete: Miranda has rescued Pug and shares his objective, yet still withholds the history that explains her unusual knowledge.

Calis and Tomas confer at Elvandar, linking the new invasion to the oldest dangers of Midkemia. Calis's mixed inheritance gives him insight into both mortal war and the Valheru legacy, while Tomas understands why any design involving ancient powers cannot be treated as a local conflict. Nakor joins Pug and Miranda's investigation with his unconventional understanding of magic. Evidence points toward Jakan and other Pantathian priests operating behind the Emerald Queen's public cause. The Queen is revered as a sacred embodiment connected to Alma-Lodaka, the creator the serpent people seek to restore, but the relationship between the woman, the goddess, and the priests controlling access to her is not yet settled.

Warnings become invasion. Fadawah's fleet reaches the Kingdom with experienced troops, siege equipment, and commanders able to adapt when individual plans fail. Political schemes and divided priorities have not stopped James and William from preparing Krondor for the worst, and Roo's supplies keep armies moving as normal trade collapses. Erik takes increasing responsibility in the field. Betrayal and infiltration weaken the defenders just as the onslaught begins, allowing the invaders to establish their campaign on Kingdom soil. Duko emerges as one of the enemy's effective human commanders, less interested in Pantathian theology than in winning the war assigned to him.

The defence of Krondor becomes a managed catastrophe. James and William know that holding the city indefinitely would trap and destroy the Kingdom's western army, so the defenders evacuate what they can and deny the invaders an intact capital. The destruction kills both men and ends the long life of James, once Jimmy the Hand, in service to the city that raised him. Prince Patrick and the surviving forces withdraw eastward. Roo escapes, but warehouses, businesses, and much of the fortune he built are swallowed by the war. Erik helps impose order on the retreat as Fadawah presses the advantage. The enemy has taken Krondor, yet the Kingdom still has an army because the defenders chose survival over a symbolic last stand.

The campaign moves through Ravensburg and Darkmoor, returning Erik to the country where his life began. Retreat, delay, and improvised defences wear down both sides. Erik's knowledge of the land and his ability to keep soldiers, horses, and supplies functioning make him central to preventing withdrawal from becoming collapse. Roo's remaining network continues to serve the army even after the commercial Krondor he knew has ceased to exist. Fadawah is forced to spend strength for every advance, while Duko and other commanders secure captured territory behind him. The Kingdom has not retaken the west, but it has denied the invaders the quick destruction on which their larger plan depended.

The invasion's concealed design is finally separated from its public story. The Emerald Queen is Jorna, Miranda's mother, made into a sacred vessel for the Pantathians' attempt to restore Alma-Lodaka; she is not an independent conqueror directing every part of the war. Jakan's use of demon forces has also exposed Midkemia to Maarg, a demon king whose appetite is greater than the serpent priests' design and whose arrival would turn their promised victory into another kind of ruin. Pug, Miranda, Nakor, Calis, and Tomas confront the interworld threat and prevent Maarg's power from taking Midkemia, breaking the supernatural core of the campaign. Miranda's hidden history is revealed fully: she is the daughter of Jorna and Macros the Black. Macros returns in a renewed body, alive again but not as the man Pug once knew. On the battlefield, Fadawah is checked rather than destroyed, and Duko retains occupied ground after Krondor's fall. James and William are dead; Patrick, Erik, and Roo survive. The Kingdom has stopped annihilation, but reclaiming the Western Realm remains the next war.

characters.description: The eldest of the three children, thoughtful, observant, and quick to take responsibility when family life changes without warning. She notices more than her brother and sister do about their parents' worries and tries to protect them while sharing their adventures around the railway.
characters.name: Roberta

characters.description: Bobbie's younger brother and the only boy among the three children. Energetic, proud, and mechanically minded, he is delighted by his model railway engine and often throws himself into a plan before considering all its consequences.
characters.name: Peter

characters.description: The youngest child, affectionate, imaginative, and inclined to say exactly what she thinks. Her innocent questions and literal interpretations often expose what the older children are trying to leave tactfully unsaid.
characters.name: Phyllis

characters.description: The children's loving and resourceful mother. After her husband is abruptly called away, she moves the family from London to a modest country house and supports them by writing stories, concealing much of her anxiety so the children can feel secure.
characters.name: Mother

characters.description: The children's affectionate father, who joins in their games and patiently repairs Peter's broken model engine. His unexplained departure with two visitors overturns the family's comfortable London life and leaves the children longing for his return.
characters.name: Father

characters.description: A railway official who confronts the children after Peter begins taking coal from the station yard. Though stern about the theft and responsible for enforcing the rules, he listens to their explanation rather than treating them as hardened wrongdoers.
characters.name: The Station Master

characters.description: A friendly porter at the country station who becomes a familiar source of railway news and practical help. Direct and proud of earning his own way, he treats the children kindly while speaking to them without ceremony.
characters.name: Albert Perks

characters.description: An elderly passenger who regularly travels past the children's field on the morning train. He begins returning their daily waves, and the children come to regard him as a distant friend even before they know his name or anything about his life.
characters.name: The Old Gentleman

characters.description: A distressed Russian exile whom the children encounter at the station. He speaks little English, has endured imprisonment far from home for his political beliefs, and has come to England hoping to find the wife and child from whom he was separated.
characters.name: The Russian Gentleman

characters.description: Perks's hardworking wife, who manages a crowded home on the porter's small income. She shares her husband's pride and is initially wary when the children's well-meant birthday project looks like condescending charity.
characters.name: Mrs Perks

characters.description: A schoolboy taking part in a paper chase near the railway, identifiable by his red jersey. He is left injured in the tunnel after the other runners have gone on, making Bobbie's watchfulness and the children's knowledge of the railway urgently important.
characters.name: Jim

recaps.ending: Bobbie's appeal to the Old Gentleman leads him to investigate Father's case. The evidence against Father is overturned, he is cleared of the charge that sent him to prison, and news of his release reaches the family. Mother prepares for his return while keeping the moment quiet. At the station, Bobbie waits as a train arrives and sees Father emerge through the steam. She runs to him, and they return together to Three Chimneys. Peter and Phyllis are reunited with him there, ending the separation that forced the family from its London home. The Old Gentleman has also become personally connected to the family through Jim, the injured schoolboy, who is his grandson. The story closes with Father restored to his wife and children and the central injustice resolved, while the friendships the children formed through the railway remain part of their new life.
recaps.in_short: When their father is suddenly taken away, Bobbie, Peter, Phyllis, and their mother leave their comfortable London home for Three Chimneys, a cottage beside a country railway. The children befriend Perks the porter, wave daily to an Old Gentleman on the train, and repeatedly turn railway life into acts of service: they help a lost Russian exile, stop a train before it strikes a landslide, aid a family whose barge catches fire, and rescue an injured schoolboy from a tunnel. Bobbie eventually learns that Father has been imprisoned after being falsely accused of betraying his country. She secretly asks the Old Gentleman for help. He investigates, the case is corrected, and Father is released. Bobbie meets him as he steps from the train, and the whole family is reunited at Three Chimneys.

recaps.text: Bobbie, Peter, and Phyllis live comfortably in London with their affectionate mother and father. Their security ends when two men visit and Father leaves with them without a proper explanation. Mother says he has been called away on business, dismisses the servants, and takes the children to a much smaller country house called Three Chimneys. Money is plainly tight, though she shields them from the reason. The nearby railway becomes the children's chief fascination. Peter's attempt to supply the cold house by taking coal from the station yard brings a stern lesson about theft. The children also begin waving each morning to an elderly passenger on the 9:15 train. When Mother falls ill and cannot afford the nourishing food ordered for her, they send the stranger a request for help. He responds generously, although Mother makes clear that they must not make a habit of asking others for things.

Since Father's unexplained departure, Bobbie, Peter, Phyllis, and Mother have moved from London to Three Chimneys beside a country railway. The children befriend Perks the porter and establish a distant friendship with the Old Gentleman who returns their waves from his regular train and helps when Mother is ill. At the station they meet a Russian exile who is confused, hungry, and unable to make himself understood in English. Mother speaks with him in French and learns that imprisonment and exile separated him from his wife and child. She takes him in, while the Old Gentleman uses his connections to help trace the missing family. Soon afterward, the children discover that a landslide has covered the track. With no time to reach the station, the girls tear up red petticoats and all three wave the pieces as danger flags. The approaching train stops just before the obstruction, saving its passengers.

The children's new life revolves around the railway after Father's unexplained disappearance and the family's move to Three Chimneys. Their friendship with the Old Gentleman has already brought help during Mother's illness and aided a Russian exile searching for his family. After Bobbie, Peter, and Phyllis stop a passenger train from striking a landslide, the railway honors their courage. Their adventures continue when a canal boat catches fire: they join the rescue effort and help bring a small child out of danger. Learning that Perks's birthday usually passes with little celebration, they collect small gifts from people throughout the village. Perks initially rejects the gathering because he believes the children have invited people to give him charity. Once he understands that the presents express genuine friendship and gratitude from neighbors who value him, his resentment gives way and the birthday celebration is restored.

Bobbie, Peter, and Phyllis have made a place for themselves around the country railway, befriending Perks and the Old Gentleman and helping others in several emergencies. Beneath those adventures, Bobbie has become increasingly aware that Mother's explanations about Father are incomplete. She finds an old newspaper report and learns the truth: Father was accused of giving state secrets to a foreign power, convicted, and sent to prison. Convinced of his innocence and unwilling to burden Mother or her siblings, Bobbie writes privately to the Old Gentleman and asks whether he can help. Meanwhile, the children watch a school paper chase whose route passes through the railway tunnel. When one runner fails to emerge, they search inside and find Jim, a boy in a red jersey, injured and unable to walk. Bobbie remains with him in the darkness while Peter and Phyllis fetch help, and Jim is carried back to Three Chimneys to recover.

After Father was taken away, Bobbie, Peter, and Phyllis moved with Mother to Three Chimneys and built a new life around the railway. They befriended Perks, appealed to the Old Gentleman when help was needed, aided a Russian exile, stopped a train before a landslide, helped at a barge fire, and rescued the injured schoolboy Jim from a tunnel. Jim proves to be the Old Gentleman's grandson, bringing their once-distant friend directly into the household. Bobbie has also discovered that Father was imprisoned after being accused of passing state secrets, and she has secretly asked the Old Gentleman to investigate because she believes Father was framed. His efforts help bring the truth to light: the conviction is overturned and Father is released. Mother prepares for his arrival, and Bobbie goes to the station. As the train's steam clears, Father steps onto the platform. Bobbie runs to meet him and brings him home, where the family is finally reunited.

characters.description: Mistress of Ingleside, home again at Glen St. Mary after three months abroad with Gilbert. Her children are growing up and need her less, and she watches the doings of the Glen, and of the new minister's family in particular, with sympathy rather than interference. She is content and no longer at the centre of her own story.
characters.name: Anne Blythe

characters.description: The Ingleside housekeeper, devoted to the Blythes and to their standing in the Glen, an authority on every family in the district and a reliable source of the news, the gossip, and the moral verdict that goes with it.
characters.name: Susan Baker

characters.description: Once Miss Cornelia Bryant of Four Winds, now married and living at the Glen, still capable, still blunt, and still convinced that men are a trial. She takes a practical interest in the neglected manse family and does more for them than the whole congregation put together.
characters.name: Mrs. Marshall Elliott

characters.description: The eldest Blythe boy, red-haired, energetic, and full of plans, who leads the children's expeditions and intends to be a soldier or an explorer or whatever else the week suggests.
characters.name: Jem Blythe

characters.description: The second Blythe boy, beautiful and dreamy, who writes verses, loves words and the look of the world, and shrinks from ugliness and violence. The other boys of the Glen think him soft; his own family know that he sees and feels more than the rest of them.
characters.name: Walter Blythe

characters.description: One of the Blythe twins, dark-eyed and serious, close to Faith and Una Meredith and inclined to take the manse children's troubles as her own.
characters.name: Nan Blythe

characters.description: Nan's twin, red-haired and quick-tempered, Jem's usual companion in the games and expeditions of Rainbow Valley.
characters.name: Di Blythe

characters.description: The youngest Blythe, a small, pretty girl who lisps, minds her clothes, and dislikes being laughed at, tagging after the older children in the valley.
characters.name: Rilla Blythe

characters.description: The new Presbyterian minister at Glen St. Mary, a widower with four children, scholarly, unworldly, and so absorbed in his books and his sermons that he does not notice the state of his house or the behaviour of his family. He is beloved in the pulpit and helpless everywhere else.
characters.name: Rev. John Meredith

characters.description: The eldest Meredith child, a sensible, self-appointed leader of his brother and sisters, quick to see when they have gone too far and equally quick to have gone there with them.
characters.name: Jerry Meredith

characters.description: The elder Meredith daughter, warm-hearted, fearless, and entirely without discretion, who acts on impulse and cannot understand why the Glen is scandalized by things that seemed perfectly reasonable at the time. She is fiercely proud of her father.
characters.name: Faith Meredith

characters.description: The younger Meredith daughter, quiet, anxious, and easily hurt, who worries about her father and her family's reputation and keeps her thoughts to herself. She is the one who notices when other people are unhappy.
characters.name: Una Meredith

characters.description: The youngest Meredith, a boy with his mother's blue eyes who collects insects, frogs, and snakes and keeps them about his person, to the horror of the congregation.
characters.name: Carl Meredith

characters.description: The Merediths' elderly housekeeper, half blind and nearly deaf, who nursed their father as a baby and will let no one else near the kitchen. Her cooking and her housekeeping are equally bad, and Mr. Meredith will not hear of dismissing her.
characters.name: Aunt Martha

characters.description: A half-starved runaway girl of about twelve found hiding in an abandoned barn, sharp-tongued, worldly, and free with information the manse children have never heard before. She has been passed from one hard household to another and has learned to look out for herself.
characters.name: Mary Vance

characters.description: One of two sisters living at a house up the hill above the harbour, a gentle, fair woman no longer young, who keeps house with her elder sister and is well liked in the Glen. She and the minister fall into conversation one evening and find they suit each other.
characters.name: Rosemary West

characters.description: Rosemary's elder sister, dark, heavy-browed, and dominant, devoted to Rosemary and determined that the two of them shall never be parted.
characters.name: Ellen West

characters.description: A loud, red-bearded, prosperous farmer of the district, famous for his temper, his opinions, and his long absence from church, who says whatever comes into his head at whatever volume it arrives.
characters.name: Norman Douglas

recaps.ending: Norman Douglas returns to church and to his old courtship of Ellen West, and the two become engaged. Ellen, marrying herself, releases Rosemary from the promise that had kept her single, and Rosemary accepts John Meredith. Una Meredith, who has been dreading a stepmother more than she could say, goes alone to Rosemary to ask her to be kind to Carl, and comes away comforted; the manse children accept the marriage and gain the mothering they have gone without. Mr. Meredith, shaken by how far his family had been neglected, is at last awake to his household. Mary Vance is settled with Mrs. Marshall Elliott and thoroughly at home in the Glen. The Blythe and Meredith children are all a year or two older, and Rainbow Valley is still theirs. The book closes with them gathered in the valley at sunset, where Walter tells them he has seen the Pied Piper coming over the hills with his music, calling the boys of the world to follow him. The others take it for one of Walter's fancies and promise lightly to follow when the call comes, and the story ends on that promise with the shadow of the coming war lying over it.
recaps.in_short: A new Presbyterian minister, the scholarly and unworldly John Meredith, comes to Glen St. Mary with four motherless children and an incompetent old housekeeper, and the manse family runs wild. Jerry, Faith, Una, and Carl make friends with the Blythe children of Ingleside and spend their days in Rainbow Valley, scandalizing the congregation with one thoughtless escapade after another while their father reads in his study and notices nothing. They rescue a starving runaway, Mary Vance, who is eventually taken in and brought up by Mrs. Marshall Elliott. Ashamed of disgracing their father, the manse children form a club to punish their own misdeeds, and one of the punishments makes Carl seriously ill, which finally wakes Mr. Meredith to his family's neglect. Meanwhile he falls in love with Rosemary West, who must refuse him because of a promise never to marry, extracted by her sister Ellen. When Ellen's own old suitor returns and marries her, Rosemary is freed and accepts the minister. The book ends with Walter Blythe's vision of the Pied Piper, a warning of the war to come.

recaps.text: Previously: Anne Shirley, brought up as an orphan at Green Gables in Avonlea, married Doctor Gilbert Blythe and lives at Ingleside in Glen St. Mary with their housekeeper Susan Baker and their children, Jem, Walter, the twins Nan and Di, Shirley, and the youngest, Rilla. Their neighbour and old friend from Four Winds days, once Miss Cornelia Bryant, is now Mrs. Marshall Elliott and lives at the Glen. The doctor's practice is long established and the family well settled. In this book Anne and Gilbert step back into the background: the story belongs to their children and to the family of the new minister at the Glen manse, and the setting is the wooded hollow below Ingleside that the children have named Rainbow Valley.

Anne comes home to Ingleside after three months in Europe, and the Glen catches her up on its news, chiefly the new Presbyterian minister. John Meredith is a widower with four children, a fine preacher, and hopelessly unpractical: the manse is dirty and disorderly, the meals are ruinous, and his old housekeeper, Aunt Martha, is half blind and will not be dismissed. Jerry, Faith, Una, and Carl Meredith are left to bring themselves up, and they do it cheerfully, running about the graveyard beside the church and making friends at once with the Blythe children in Rainbow Valley, the wooded hollow below Ingleside. Exploring an abandoned barn, the children find a half-starved girl of about twelve hiding there. Mary Vance has run away from a hard mistress and has nowhere to go; the manse children feed her and take her in, without troubling to consult their father.

Mary Vance is installed at the manse, where she is useful, sharp-tongued, and a good deal too well informed for the taste of the Glen. Her situation is settled when it emerges that the woman she ran from cannot claim her, and Mrs. Marshall Elliott takes her to bring up, giving Mary a home and the Glen a steady supply of comment. The manse children go on disgracing their father without meaning to: they play in the graveyard, keep house on the wrong day, and appear at church in whatever they happen to be wearing, and the congregation talks. Mr. Meredith, absorbed in his books, sees none of it. Walking home one evening he falls into conversation with Rosemary West, one of two sisters who keep house up the hill, and finds himself talking easily for the first time since his wife died. He begins to visit the hill house, and Ellen West watches the friendship with growing unease.

The manse children learn how badly the Glen speaks of them and are horrified, less for themselves than for their father, and they form a club to keep themselves in order, with the rule that any of them who does wrong shall choose and carry out their own punishment. The penalties are as ill-judged as the offences: they go without meals, walk to church in disgrace, and set themselves ordeals no adult would have permitted. Faith goes on acting first and thinking afterwards, in one case riding a neighbour's pig through the village for a wager, and afterwards, when the congregation blames her father for her behaviour, standing up in church to explain herself to the whole assembly, which scandalizes the Glen more than the original offence. Walter Blythe, who hates fighting, fights an older boy who has insulted Faith and his own mother, and is respected afterwards by boys who had thought him a coward.

John Meredith at last asks Rosemary West to marry him. She refuses, and cannot tell him why: years ago, when Ellen gave up her own chance of marriage to keep house for her sister, Rosemary promised never to leave her. The minister, humiliated and baffled, keeps away from the hill house, and Rosemary is left as unhappy as he is. When she tells Ellen what she has given up, the two sisters quarrel and settle into a cold silence. Faith and Una, learning something of the courtship, are torn between wanting their father happy and dreading a stepmother, and Una in particular is wretched about it. The manse runs on as badly as ever, and Mary Vance, from her comfortable place with Mrs. Marshall Elliott, keeps the children supplied with the Glen's opinion of them.

One of the club's self-imposed penalties goes badly wrong. Carl, punishing himself for a fault, spends a whole night alone in the graveyard in the cold, is brought home ill, and his illness turns dangerous. His father, sitting up with him, understands for the first time how far he has let his children go untended, and is bitterly ashamed of it. Carl recovers, and Mr. Meredith is a better father afterwards for the shock of it. Into this comes Norman Douglas, a loud, red-bearded farmer who has stayed away from church for years and who takes it into his head to come back, and to renew a courtship he abandoned in his youth.

Norman Douglas courts Ellen West as noisily as he does everything else, and Ellen, who refused him long ago, accepts him. Marrying herself, she can no longer hold Rosemary to the promise she exacted, and she releases her outright. Rosemary and John Meredith are reconciled and engaged, and the manse is to have a mistress at last. Una Meredith, still frightened of what a stepmother may mean, goes alone to Rosemary to beg her to be good to Carl, and Rosemary's answer settles the children's fears. Mary Vance is at home with Mrs. Marshall Elliott and as talkative as ever. On a still evening the children gather in Rainbow Valley, and Walter tells them that he has seen the Pied Piper coming down over the hills, playing, and that one day he will call and the boys will have to follow him. The others laugh and promise to go when the call comes, and the book ends there.
